title: The Karpman Drama Triangle: How to Stop Playing Victim in Your Own Team
author: The Good Boss
summary: Drawing on a personal story about a manager who habitually turned every problem his team raised into his own crusade (and even claimed their burnout as his own), this piece introduces the Karpman Drama Triangle — a framework originally developed by psychiatrist Stephen Karpman in 1968 from studying fairy tales and stage drama, not workplace dynamics. The three roles it identifies — Victim, Persecutor, and Rescuer — are shown to recur constantly in team dynamics: the manager in the author's opening story is a textbook Rescuer, someone who inserts himself into problems that don't need rescuing and effectively steals the team's agency to solve their own issues. The piece maps a specific destructive cycle: a leader rescues by lowering the bar, the team starts to feel like victims of low expectations, the leader gets frustrated and slides into persecutor mode, and the team disengages and burns out, repeating the loop. Its underlying claim for leaders is that self-awareness of which corner of the triangle you're standing in, in a given conversation, is what actually breaks the cycle rather than generic management advice like 'set expectations and move on.'
points: Traces the framework's surprising origin: Karpman developed it in 1968 studying fairy tales and stage drama, not office politics — which is why the same three roles recur everywhere.
Names the three roles precisely: the Victim ('poor me, nobody helps me'), the Persecutor (the critic with impossible standards), and the Rescuer (fixes problems nobody asked them to fix).
Uses a personal story of a 'rescuer' boss who turned every team problem into his own crusade — even claiming the team's burnout as his own experience — to make the pattern concrete.
Maps a repeating destructive cycle: rescue by lowering the bar to victim resentment to persecutor frustration to team disengagement, and back to rescue.
quotes: Almost every week, he would tell me some version of 'I'm the only one fighting for the team.' Every problem we raised to him quickly turned into his problem, and then somehow, into his personal mission.

Karpman wasn't studying office politics or leadership philosophies. Not at all. He was actually studying fairy tales and stage drama. Karpman noticed that basically every story — whether Little Red Riding Hood, soap operas, or even your family's Thanksgiving dinner — features the same three characters, or 'roles', showing up over and over again.

The Rescuer. This is the one who pops in to 'fix things' like it's their problem. But in most cases, the rescuer tries to rescue a situation that doesn't need rescuing at all. He tries to help people who didn't really ask for help.

You rescue your team by lowering the bar. They feel like victim of your low expectations. You get frustrated with that, and become the persecutor. The team gets frustrated, disengaged, and burnt out. Rise and repeat.

The value of learning this framework is to become more self-aware and team-aware. You want to be able to detect when you're playing one of those roles of the drama triangle, and how you get out of that trap.
